courses.title: Latkes, four ways
courses.intro: Potato latkes fried in oil are the classic; sweet potato and zucchini latkes add color, and the sheet-pan version saves standing at the stove. Applesauce from scratch takes about 30 minutes.

courses.title: Brisket and other mains
courses.intro: Brisket is the centerpiece in many American Jewish homes, and it is best made a day ahead. A roast chicken or a pot of chicken soup are other family favorites.

courses.title: Kugel, vegetables and challah
courses.intro: Potato kugel for a meat meal and sweet noodle kugel for a dairy one, a sweet tzimmes, something green, and a braided challah.

courses.title: A dairy meal
courses.intro: Many families also eat cheese and other dairy foods during Hanukkah, a custom tied to the story of Judith. Blintzes, cheese pancakes and noodle kugel make a dairy supper with latkes and sour cream.

courses.title: Doughnuts and fried sweets
courses.intro: Sufganiyot, jelly doughnuts, are the Hanukkah treat in Israel; bimuelos, honey-soaked fritters, come from Sephardic kitchens.

onion-braised-brisket.ahead_part: braise the brisket, chill it, then slice it cold

cheese-blintzes.ahead_part: make the crepes and fill them

sufganiyot.ahead_part: make the dough and let it rise slowly in the refrigerator overnight

howmuch.note: It shrinks by about a third to a half as it braises.
3 lb of apples makes about 4 cups.

recipes.name: Classic Potato Latkes
recipes.summary: Crisp, lacy-edged potato pancakes fried in oil, the best-known Hanukkah food in many Ashkenazi Jewish homes. Serve with applesauce, sour cream, or both.
equipment: box grater or food processor with a grating disk
large heavy skillet (cast iron is ideal)
baking sheet with a wire rack

ingredients.prep: for frying; about ¼ inch in the pan

steps: Heat the oven to 200°F and set a wire rack in a baking sheet. Frying safety: use a heavy pan, keep the oil below smoking (350 to 375°F), and never leave hot oil alone. Keep a lid or sheet pan beside the stove; if the oil catches fire, turn off the burner and slide the lid over it. Never pour water on a grease fire. Keep children back from the stove.
Grate the potatoes and onion on the large holes of a box grater or in a food processor, alternating them; the onion helps keep the potatoes from turning gray.

Squeeze the grated potatoes hard in a clean kitchen towel, a handful at a time, over a bowl. Dry potatoes make crisp latkes, and less water means less spattering oil. Let the squeezed-out liquid sit 5 minutes, pour off the water and keep the white potato starch at the bottom of the bowl.
Mix the potatoes and onion with the starch, eggs, flour, salt, pepper and baking powder.
Heat about ¼ inch of oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until a shred of potato sizzles right away (about 350 to 375°F).

Drop in heaping 2-tablespoon mounds, a few at a time without crowding, and flatten them to about 3 inches. Fry 3 to 4 minutes per side, until deep golden brown and crisp. Lower the heat if they brown too fast.

Drain briefly on paper towels, then move to the rack in the oven. Keep finished latkes warm and crisp in one layer on a wire rack set in a baking sheet in a 200°F oven while you fry the rest. Stir the batter between batches and add oil as needed, letting it heat back up.
Serve hot with applesauce and sour cream. When you’re done, turn off the burner and let the oil cool completely before throwing it away in a sealed container.
recipes.make_ahead: Fry up to a day ahead, cool on the rack and refrigerate; recrisp on a rack at 400°F, 8 to 10 minutes. Or freeze them.

freezer.text: Freeze fried, cooled latkes in one layer, then bag them, up to 3 months. Reheat from frozen at 400°F, about 12 minutes.

leftovers.text: Refrigerate within 2 hours; keep up to 3 days. Recrisp on a rack at 400°F for 8 to 10 minutes; a microwave makes them soggy.

recipes.kids: Kids can mix the batter and spoon on toppings. Grating knuckles and hot oil are grown-up jobs.

swaps.gluten_free: Use potato starch or a gluten-free flour in place of the flour or matzo meal.
swaps.egg_free: Leave out the eggs and add 2 more tablespoons flour; handle them gently.
swaps.kosher_meat_meal: For a meat meal, serve with applesauce instead of sour cream.

prep_day.ahead: Fry and freeze ahead, or recrisp the next day.

recipes.name: Sweet Potato Latkes
recipes.summary: Orange, slightly sweet latkes from grated sweet potato with a little cinnamon and green onion. They brown faster than potato latkes, so fry them over medium heat.
equipment: baking sheet with a wire rack
steps: Heat the oven to 200°F and set a wire rack in a baking sheet. Frying safety: use a heavy pan, keep the oil below smoking (350 to 375°F), and never leave hot oil alone. Keep a lid or sheet pan beside the stove; if the oil catches fire, turn off the burner and slide the lid over it. Never pour water on a grease fire. Keep children back from the stove.
Grate the sweet potatoes on the large holes. Squeeze them lightly in a towel; they hold less water than white potatoes.
Mix with the green onions, eggs, flour, salt, cinnamon and pepper.

Heat ¼ inch of oil over medium heat. Fry heaping 2-tablespoon mounds, flattened, 3 minutes per side, until browned and crisp at the edges. Sweet potatoes have more sugar and burn faster; turn the heat down if needed.
Drain on paper towels, then keep warm on the rack in the oven. Serve with sour cream and a drizzle of honey.
recipes.make_ahead: Fry a day ahead, refrigerate, and recrisp at 400°F on a rack.

freezer.text: Freeze in one layer, then bag, up to 3 months; reheat at 400°F.

leftovers.text: Refrigerate within 2 hours; keep up to 3 days. Recrisp on a rack at 400°F for 8 to 10 minutes; a microwave makes them soggy.

recipes.kids: Kids can mix the batter and drizzle the honey.

swaps.savory: Leave out the cinnamon and add ½ teaspoon cumin and some chopped cilantro.
swaps.gluten_free: Use potato starch instead of flour.

recipes.name: Zucchini and Carrot Latkes
recipes.summary: Light vegetable fritters with zucchini, carrot, a little potato and fresh dill. A colorful latke for a dairy meal with a yogurt dip.
steps: Toss the zucchini with 1 teaspoon of the salt in a colander and let it drain 10 minutes. Then squeeze the zucchini, carrot and potato very dry in a towel.

Frying safety: use a heavy pan, keep the oil below smoking (350 to 375°F), and never leave hot oil alone. Keep a lid or sheet pan beside the stove; if the oil catches fire, turn off the burner and slide the lid over it. Never pour water on a grease fire. Keep children back from the stove.
Mix the vegetables with the green onions, dill, eggs, flour, pepper and the remaining salt.
Heat ¼ inch of oil over medium-high. Fry 2-tablespoon mounds, flattened, 3 minutes per side until golden. Drain on paper towels and keep warm in a 200°F oven.
Stir the yogurt, garlic and lemon juice together for dipping.
recipes.make_ahead: Grate the carrots a day ahead. Make the yogurt dip up to 3 days ahead.

freezer.text: Freeze fried latkes up to 2 months; recrisp at 400°F.

leftovers.text: Refrigerate within 2 hours; keep up to 3 days. Recrisp on a rack at 400°F for 8 to 10 minutes; a microwave makes them soggy.

recipes.kids: Kids can squeeze the vegetables in the towel (a good arm workout) and stir the dip.

swaps.dairy_free: Serve with applesauce instead of the yogurt dip.

prep_day.ahead: Grate the carrots; make the dip.

recipes.name: Oven-Baked Sheet-Pan Latkes
recipes.summary: Latkes baked in a very hot oven on oiled pans: less oil, no spattering, and every batch done at once. Crisp edges with a softer middle.
steps: Heat the oven to 450°F with racks in the upper and lower thirds. Pour 2 tablespoons of oil onto each baking sheet and tilt to coat. Heat the pans in the oven 5 minutes.
Grate the potatoes and onion. Squeeze the grated potatoes hard in a clean kitchen towel, a handful at a time, over a bowl. Dry potatoes make crisp latkes, and less water means less spattering oil.
Mix with the eggs, flour, salt and pepper.
Carefully take out the hot pans. Drop 2-tablespoon mounds on them, flatten to 3 inches, and brush the tops with the remaining oil.
Bake 15 minutes, until browned underneath. Flip, swap the pans between racks and bake 10 to 15 minutes more, until crisp and golden.
recipes.make_ahead: Bake a day ahead and recrisp at 400°F on a rack.

freezer.text: Freeze baked latkes up to 3 months; reheat at 400°F.

leftovers.text: Refrigerate within 2 hours; keep up to 3 days. Recrisp on a rack at 400°F for 8 to 10 minutes; a microwave makes them soggy.

recipes.kids: Kids can mix and shape the latkes on the cool pan corners with a grown-up placing them on the hot pans.

swaps.gluten_free: Use potato starch instead of flour.

recipes.name: Sufganiyot (Jelly Doughnuts)
recipes.summary: Soft, yeasted doughnuts fried golden, filled with jam and dusted with powdered sugar. In Israel they are the Hanukkah treat; they take an afternoon, mostly waiting for the dough to rise.
equipment: stand mixer with dough hook, or a large bowl
2½- to 3-inch round cutter or a glass
large heavy pot or Dutch oven
piping bag with a round tip, or a zip-top bag
a lid or sheet pan that covers the pot
steps: Stir the warm milk, yeast and 1 tablespoon of the sugar together; let stand 5 to 10 minutes until foamy.

Mix in the remaining sugar, the flour, salt, eggs, butter and vanilla. Knead 6 to 8 minutes (or 5 minutes with a dough hook) until soft, smooth and slightly tacky. Add a spoonful of flour only if it’s very sticky.
Cover and let rise in a warm spot 1 to 1½ hours, until doubled.
Roll the dough ½ inch thick on a floured counter and cut rounds. Set them on floured parchment, cover loosely and let rise 30 to 45 minutes, until puffy. Reroll the scraps once.

Frying safety: use a heavy pan, keep the oil below smoking (about 350°F), and never leave hot oil alone. Keep a lid or sheet pan beside the stove; if the oil catches fire, turn off the burner and slide the lid over it. Never pour water on a grease fire. Keep children back from the stove. Use a deep pot with oil about 2 inches deep and at least 3 inches of room above it.

Heat the oil to 350°F. Fry 3 or 4 doughnuts at a time, lowering them in gently by hand-holding the parchment edge or with the spider, 1½ to 2 minutes per side, until deep golden. Hotter oil browns the outside before the inside cooks; keep it near 350°F.
Drain on a rack. Tear the first one open to check that the center is cooked through, not doughy; fry the rest a little longer if needed.
When cool enough to handle, poke a hole in the side of each with a skewer or chopstick, wiggle it to make a pocket, and pipe in about 2 teaspoons of jam. Dust with powdered sugar.
Turn off the burner and let the oil cool completely before straining or throwing it away in a sealed container.
recipes.make_ahead: Make the dough the night before and let it rise slowly in the refrigerator; let it warm for 30 minutes before rolling. Doughnuts are best the day they’re fried.

freezer.text: Freeze unfilled doughnuts up to 1 month; thaw, warm at 350°F for 5 minutes, then fill and dust.

leftovers.text: Keep at room temperature, loosely covered, for 1 day.

recipes.kids: Kids can cut out the rounds, poke the jam holes in cooled doughnuts and shake on the powdered sugar. The frying is for grown-ups.

swaps.baked: For a lower-oil version, bake the risen rounds at 375°F for 10 to 12 minutes, brush with melted butter and roll in sugar before filling; they’ll be softer and more like rolls.
swaps.fillings: Try lemon curd, chocolate spread or a thick vanilla custard.
swaps.dairy_free: Use water or oat milk and oil instead of milk and butter.

prep_day.ahead: Make the dough the night before.

recipes.name: Bimuelos (Honey Fritters)
recipes.summary: Light, puffy yeasted fritters drizzled with warm honey syrup and cinnamon, eaten at Hanukkah in many Sephardic Jewish families. No rolling or cutting: the batter goes straight into the oil by the spoonful.
equipment: a lid or sheet pan that covers the pot
steps: Whisk the flour, yeast, sugar and salt. Stir in the warm water to make a thick, sticky batter. Cover and let rise in a warm place about 1 hour, until doubled and bubbly.

Frying safety: use a heavy pan, keep the oil below smoking (about 365°F), and never leave hot oil alone. Keep a lid or sheet pan beside the stove; if the oil catches fire, turn off the burner and slide the lid over it. Never pour water on a grease fire. Keep children back from the stove. Use a deep pot with oil about 2 inches deep and plenty of room above it.
Heat the oil to 365°F. Wet two spoons and drop walnut-size blobs of batter into the oil, a few at a time. Fry 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until puffed and golden all over. Drain on the rack.
Warm the honey, water and lemon juice until runny. Drizzle over the fritters and dust with cinnamon. Serve warm.
Turn off the burner and let the oil cool completely before throwing it away.
recipes.make_ahead: Best fresh. Mix the batter an hour before you want to fry.
recipes.kids: Kids can stir the batter, watch it rise, and drizzle the honey.

swaps.sugar_syrup: Use simple syrup with a strip of orange peel instead of honey, or roll them in cinnamon sugar.

recipes.name: Onion-Braised Brisket
recipes.summary: A beef brisket browned and braised slowly on a thick bed of onions with tomato, garlic and broth until fork-tender. Like many braises, it tastes best made a day ahead, chilled, sliced and reheated in its gravy.
recipes.serving_size: about 4 oz sliced brisket with onions and gravy
equipment: large Dutch oven or roasting pan with a tight lid (or heavy foil)

ingredients.prep: first cut (flat), with a thin layer of fat

steps: Heat the oven to 325°F. Pat the brisket dry and rub it all over with the salt, pepper and paprika. Wash your hands.
Heat the oil in the Dutch oven over medium-high and brown the brisket well, 5 to 6 minutes per side (cut it in half to fit if needed). Set it aside on a plate.
Lower the heat to medium, add the onions and cook, stirring and scraping up the browned bits, 12 to 15 minutes, until soft and golden. Stir in the garlic and tomato paste for 1 minute.
Stir in the broth, tomatoes, brown sugar, vinegar, bay leaves and thyme. Set the brisket fat side up on the onions, tuck the carrots around, and spoon some onions over the top.
Cover tightly and braise 3½ to 4 hours, until a fork slides in with almost no resistance. Beef is safe at 145°F (USDA); brisket is cooked far beyond that, near 200°F, to become tender.

Make it ahead (the usual way): cool the brisket in its liquid for up to an hour, then refrigerate it, covered, overnight. The next day lift off the hardened fat, slice the cold meat across the grain about ¼ inch thick, and lay the slices back in the gravy.
Reheat covered at 325°F for 45 to 60 minutes, until the gravy bubbles and the center slices reach 165°F. Pull out the bay leaves and thyme stems and serve with the onions and gravy.
Serving it the same day instead: rest the brisket 20 minutes, skim the fat from the gravy, then slice across the grain.
recipes.make_ahead: Braise up to 2 days ahead and refrigerate in its gravy; slice cold and reheat to 165°F.

freezer.text: Freeze sliced brisket in its gravy up to 3 months. Thaw in the refrigerator and reheat to 165°F.

leftovers.text: Refrigerate within 2 hours; eat within 3 to 4 days (USDA). Reheat to 165°F. Great on challah the next day.

recipes.kids: Kids can rub the spices on (then wash hands well), tuck in the carrots, and help peel the onions.

swaps.slow_cooker: Brown the meat and onions, then cook everything in a slow cooker on low 8 to 10 hours.
swaps.sweet_and_sour: Use ½ cup ketchup in place of the crushed tomatoes and add ¼ cup more brown sugar.

prep_day.ahead: Braise the brisket a day ahead; chill, slice and reheat in the gravy.

recipes.name: Crispy Potato Kugel
recipes.summary: A golden baked pudding of grated potatoes and sweet sautéed onions, crisp on top and at the edges and tender inside. Like latkes, but all in one pan.
steps: Heat the oven to 400°F. Cook the chopped onion in 2 tablespoons of the oil until golden, about 10 minutes.
Pour 2 tablespoons of oil into the baking dish and put it in the oven to heat while you grate.
Grate the potatoes and the second onion. Squeeze them dry in a towel, a handful at a time.
Mix the potatoes with the cooked onion, eggs, flour, salt, pepper and the remaining oil.

Carefully take out the hot dish and spread the potato mixture in it; it should sizzle. Bake 60 to 75 minutes, until deep golden and crisp on top and a knife slides easily into the center (it reaches well past 160°F, done for an egg dish).
Let it rest 10 minutes and cut into squares.
recipes.make_ahead: Bake up to 2 days ahead. Reheat uncovered at 375°F for 20 to 25 minutes, until hot (165°F) and crisp again.

freezer.text: Freeze baked squares up to 3 months; reheat from frozen at 375°F.

leftovers.text: Refrigerate within 2 hours; eat within 3 to 4 days (USDA). Reheat to 165°F.

recipes.kids: Kids can beat the eggs and mix everything with a big spoon.

swaps.gluten_free: Use potato starch instead of flour.

recipes.name: Carrot and Sweet Potato Tzimmes
recipes.summary: Carrots and sweet potatoes baked with dried apricots and raisins in orange juice and honey until glazed and tender. A sweet side that sits happily beside brisket.
steps: Heat the oven to 375°F.
Toss everything together in the baking dish.
Cover with foil and bake 40 minutes. Uncover, stir, and bake 20 to 25 minutes more, stirring once, until the vegetables are tender and glazed.
recipes.make_ahead: Bake up to 2 days ahead; reheat covered at 350°F until hot.

leftovers.text: Refrigerate within 2 hours; eat within 3 to 4 days (USDA). Reheat to 165°F.

recipes.kids: Kids can measure and toss everything in the pan.

swaps.prunes: Prunes are a traditional addition; use them in place of the apricots.

recipes.name: Cheese Blintzes
recipes.summary: Thin crepes wrapped around a lightly sweet ricotta and cream cheese filling, browned in butter. A favorite for a dairy meal at Hanukkah, served with sour cream and berries or applesauce.

ingredients.prep: melted, plus more for the pan

steps: Blend the crepe ingredients until smooth and let the batter rest 30 minutes (or overnight in the refrigerator).

Heat the skillet over medium and brush with butter. Pour in about 3 tablespoons batter and swirl to coat the bottom thinly. Cook about 1 minute, until the top is set and the edge lifts; cook on one side only. Slide it out, browned side up, and repeat, stacking the crepes.
Mix the filling ingredients until smooth.
Spoon 2 tablespoons filling onto the browned side of each crepe near one edge. Fold in the sides, then roll up like a little package.

Heat the oven to 375°F. Melt the butter in a skillet over medium heat and brown the blintzes seam side down first, 2 minutes per side. Move them to the baking dish and bake 10 to 12 minutes, until the filling is hot, 160°F, since it contains raw egg (USDA).
Serve warm with sour cream and berries or applesauce.
recipes.make_ahead: Fill and roll the blintzes up to a day ahead and refrigerate, or freeze them; brown and bake when ready.

freezer.text: Freeze filled, unbrowned blintzes in one layer, then bag, up to 3 months. Brown from frozen and bake 20 minutes, to 160°F.

leftovers.text: Refrigerate within 2 hours; eat within 3 days. Reheat at 350°F until hot (165°F).

recipes.kids: Kids can stir the filling and roll up the blintzes (the folding is like wrapping a present).

swaps.cottage_cheese: Use small-curd cottage cheese, drained and pressed through a strainer, in place of the ricotta.
swaps.fruit: Fill with thick cooked apples or cherries instead of cheese.

prep_day.ahead: Make the crepes and fill them.

recipes.name: Leftover Brisket Sandwiches on Challah
recipes.summary: The next day’s best meal: brisket slices warmed in their gravy and piled on thick slices of challah with a little horseradish and the sweet braised onions.

ingredients.prep: leftover onion-braised brisket, sliced, with ½ cup of its gravy and onions

steps: Warm the brisket slices in their gravy and onions in a covered pan over medium-low heat, 6 to 8 minutes, until steaming and 165°F (USDA).
Toast the challah lightly if you like. Spread with horseradish.
Pile on the brisket and onions, add greens or pickles, and close the sandwiches. Spoon a little gravy on top for dipping.

freezer.text: Freeze the brisket, not the sandwiches.

recipes.kids: Kids can build their own sandwiches; skip the horseradish for them.

swaps.latke_sandwich: Use two latkes instead of bread for a latke-brisket sandwich.
